context: Al-Ikhlas came down as an answer. The transmitted reports, graded fair by many scholars, relate that questioners demanded of the Prophet ﷺ, unsub lana rabbaka, trace your Lord’s lineage for us, idolaters of Makkah in one report, and in another, questioners in Madinah, which is why the scholars differ over its Makkan or Madinan origin. The surah replied with a definition that refuses all lineage: He is Allah, Ahad, uniquely One; as-Samad, the self-sufficient on whom all depend; He neither begets nor is begotten, and none is equal to Him.

No surah saturated the Prophet’s ﷺ daily worship more. He paired it with Al-Kafirun in the sunnah of Fajr and the rak’ahs after tawaf, sealed his witr with it, and recited the three Quls over his palms each night. When a commander of an expedition ended every recitation with it and was asked why, he said: because it is the description of ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it. Tell him, said the Prophet ﷺ, that Allah loves him.
name_story: Al-Ikhlas means pure sincerity, and the surah never uses the word: it earned the name by being purely about Allah, no command, no story, no other subject, and by purifying the creed of whoever holds it. It is also cited as Qul huwa Allahu Ahad from its opening, and some early books call it Surat at-Tawhid, the surah of divine oneness.

movements.note: The identity is stated in two names: Ahad, One without division or series, and as-Samad, the eternal refuge whom all creation needs and who needs nothing.
The negations that guard the affirmation: no offspring and no origin, and none in all existence is kufuwan, equal or comparable, to Him.

themes.d: Ahad is not the first of a series but the One who admits no series: unique in essence, names, and deeds, beyond division and beyond counting.
Every creature leans on Him for every breath while He leans on nothing: the name that turns all human dependency into an address.
Lam yalid wa lam yulad: the surah fences the truth against every mythology of divine families, and against every subtle modern idol.
The Quran teaches creed, law, and the accounts of nations; this surah carries the creed whole, which is how the scholars explained its equivalence to a third.

heart: Al-Ikhlas recited slowly is the heart returning to its one fixed point. Four verses, and every direction of human worship is corrected at once: Ahad dissolves the crowded pantheons, ancient and modern, and as-Samad quietly redirects all our leaning, on salaries, on people, on our own competence, toward the only support that does not itself need supporting. The reciter feels the surah working like a plumb line dropped through the self, truing whatever had tilted toward created things during the day.

Its shortness is its mercy and its test. Said in seconds, it can pass unweighed; said with presence, it is the heaviest speech a tongue can carry, the description of ar-Rahman by ar-Rahman. The Companion who could not stop reciting it was told that Allah loved him, and that door is not closed: love of this surah is love of the One it describes, and He answers it in kind.

passages.why: The Quran’s definition of God in His own words: hear Ahad and let it empty every false throne.
As-Samad: the name to lean on when every created support has bent.
The final fence: none is equal to Him, the verse that completes the creed in seven words.

connections.why: Al-Kafirun and Al-Ikhlas travel together in the Prophet’s ﷺ prayer: the first is disavowal of every false god, the second the description of the true One.
Al-Falaq begins the two refuges that follow: after the creed is pure, the believer is taught to shelter it.

virtue.text: The Prophet ﷺ said that Qul huwa Allahu Ahad equals a third of the Quran, a sound and famous virtue, and he ﷺ told the man who loved it because it describes ar-Rahman: Allah loves him.
virtue.src: Bukhari 5013, Muslim 811; the love report, Bukhari 7375
